precepts.text: There was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, a mighty man of power; and he had a son, whose name was Saul. So Saul and Mordecai come out of the same line. This was not a regular line; this was a mighty Benjamite line. Keep that in mind for what follows.
precepts.point: Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite: Mordecai and Esther were of the tribe of Benjamin.

note.label: Nolan Wells: The Perpetual Hatred We Never Learned

precepts.why:
Esther 2:5 gives Mordecai’s line: “a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite.” Mordecai, and Esther with him, were of the tribe of Benjamin. Go back to 1 Samuel 9 and see who Kish is.

“Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power.” Kish was a mighty man of power.

“And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people.”

So Saul and Mordecai come out of the same line, the line of Kish. This was not a regular line; this was a mighty Benjamite line. Keep that in mind for what follows, because the enemy Saul was sent against in his day, the Amalekites and their king Agag, shows up again in Mordecai’s day. The hatred is perpetual, and it runs down the same lines.

precepts.text: Saul answered, am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? Benjamin was the smallest because of the judgment poured out in this war.
precepts.point: That judgment is why Saul, in the days of the first king, calls himself a Benjamite of the smallest of the tribes of Israel; this war is what minimized the tribe. There have been mighty and righteous Benjamites since, Paul chief among them, but it is written, and we learn the history as it is written.

note.label: Judges 20: Israel's War Against Benjamin

precepts.why:
Jump ahead to the days of the first king and hear how a Benjamite speaks of his own tribe. When Samuel comes to him, Saul answers, “Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?”

Benjamin was the smallest of the tribes of Israel because of the judgment poured out in this war. Only “six hundred men turned and fled to the wilderness unto the rock Rimmon, and abode in the rock Rimmon four months”; that remnant is all that kept the tribe from being utterly destroyed. Everything else, “the men of every city, as the beast, and all that came to hand”, was smitten “with the edge of the sword”, and the cities were set on fire.

Benjamin was judged big time. The Most High pushed the reset button on the tribe for the sodomite and rape activity that came out of Gibeah, and chapter 21 shows the drastic measures that had to be taken so Benjamin could continue producing as a tribe. That is the war that minimized the tribe, and that is why Saul calls himself a Benjamite of the smallest of the tribes.

There have been mighty and righteous Benjamites since, Paul chief among them. But it is written, and we learn the history as it is written.

precepts.text: When the children struggled together within Rebekah, she went to enquire of the Lord; in that time, going to enquire of the Lord meant going to a seer.
precepts.point: Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.

note.label: 1 Samuel 9: Saul Is Led to Samuel the Seer

precepts.why:
When the children struggled together within Rebekah, “she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to enquire of the Lord.”

In that time, going to enquire of the Lord meant going to a seer. That is what Samuel explains: “Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.”

So Saul and his servant went to the man of God, “an honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass”, bringing the fourth part of a shekel of silver, that he might “tell us our way.”

precepts.text: Man's goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way?
precepts.point: Saul thought he was going out to fetch his father's asses, but his purpose was to be led unto Samuel; the Lord had already told Samuel he was sending him.

note.label: 1 Samuel 9: Saul Is Led to Samuel the Seer

precepts.why:
“Man’s goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way?”

Saul thought he was going out to fetch his father's asses, but his purpose was to be led unto Samuel. The Lord had already told Samuel in his ear a day before: “To morrow about this time I will send thee a man out of the land of Benjamin, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel.”

Saul did not understand his own way; his goings were of the Lord. “And when Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said unto him, Behold the man whom I spake to thee of! this same shall reign over my people.”

precepts.text: Saul had answered, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me? That was the little-in-his-own-sight attitude Saul started with.
precepts.point: And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in Deuteronomy 25. Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
“When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel?” Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance.

That is how Saul started. He had answered Samuel, “Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?” That was the little-in-his-own-sight attitude: he thought nothing of himself, with no confidence to be a ruler, and the Most High still chose him.

Then the Lord sent him on the errand of the vengeance written in Deuteronomy 25: “Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed.” “Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?” Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

points: To morrow about this time I will send thee a man out of the land of Benjamin, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines. That he may save God's people out of the hands of the Philistines. I want to highlight that.

So we are in here and God has chosen each of you mighty men to be the saviours of the nation of Israel in these last days. I hope y'all understand that y'all are not here to be anything short of the saviours of the nation of Israel. That is what you are. That is who you have been called to be. The same exact way we are reading about King Saul, because King Saul never fought a battle by himself. So what were all those men who were battling as well? They were saviours.

From his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people. Saul was the top of the food chain, the cream of the crop, thus saith the Lord.

note.label: The Bold and the Bashful

note.label: The Bold and the Bashful

points: When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said unto him, Behold the man whom I spake to thee of; this same shall reign over my people. Saul was the man the Lord himself chose.

note.label: The Bold and the Bashful

points: And Saul answered, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Wherefore then speakest thou so to me? What did Saul think of himself?

Notice something, brothers: the leadership will see the best in you, and you will not even see it for yourself, because you have that low self-esteem. We will see greatness in you, and you say, I am just a soldier, I am just an officer of ten, I cannot do anything, I am just going to blend in and not maximize my potential. Some of you are in this Saul spirit right here: bashfulness, lack of confidence, low self-esteem, scared to make a mistake, scared of correction and rebuke. But how did the Lord see King Saul? Go back to verse 2: there was not a goodlier person than he.
